newsitem.title: USA: SEC sues for fraud over blood-sugar device claims.
newsitem.headline: SEC sues for fraud over blood-sugar device claims.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission Monday charged a Gaithersburg, Md., company with fraud for allegedly falsely claiming it had developed a device that could accurately predict a person's blood sugar content.

In a civil complaint filed in a federal district court here, the SEC alleged that Futrex Inc made the claims in a private financing drive that raised $1.85 million in 1994 and in a proposed initial offering of common stock in 1995 that aimed at raising $18 million.
The offering documents were distributed to nearly 20,000 potential investors but Futrex later postponed the IPO.

The SEC said that in both efforts, Futrex and its president, Robert Rosenthal, claimed that Futrex' hand-held "Dream Beam" analyzer could measure and accurately predict a person's blood glucose level by passing infrared light through the finger. Rosenthal is also a defendant in the case.

The SEC is seeking injuctions against further securities law violations by the defendants, an order that Futrex offer to compensate the investors in the private placement and civil monetary penalties against Rosenthal.
Futrex and its lawyer were not available to comment on the case.
In its lawsuit, the SEC alleged that no Futrex employee had ever reviewed or analyzed any data to support the claims that the Dream Beam analyzer actually works.
In offering documents for its proposed public offering, the SEC alleged that Futrex claimed that a 1991 study it conducted found that another device it had developed was "technically feasible."

The SEC alleged the claim was false and misleading because Rosenthal used data selectively to make the pitch believable and the study itself did not involve any attempt to use the infrared analyzer to predict blood glucose levels.

Between 10 to 20 units of the device cited in the study, Futrex 9000, were sold abroad but most of those were returned, the SEC said, adding the devices were not capable of measuring blood glucose levels.
The fact that the devices were returned was not disclosed in the stock offering documents, the SEC said.

The SEC also alleged that field studies said to have been made in 1994 and 1995 by the company were false and misleading and that data generated by the 1995 tests was useless because of a manufacturing defect in all the Dream Beams.
But Rosenthal ordered his staff to proceeed with the tests to avoid the embarrasing disclosure of the manufacturing defect to participants in the studies, the SEC said.

In some meetings with prospective investors, Rosenthal allegedly demonstrated that a Dream Beam showed his correct blood glucose level. But the demonstrations were staged to deceive potential investors, the SEC alleged.
